zh.question: 从太空一直靠近，所有星球最后都会出现可以站立的地面吗？
zh.observe: 先比较公转和大小，再选择地球播放云层动态，选择沙漠或冰盖，再拖动下降进度。换成木星，看风暴与更浓的大气；选择太阳找黑子和日珥。最后从土星进入土卫六，再回到土星系统。

academic.title: 公转是持续改变方向
academic.body: 行星具有运动速度，同时受太阳引力作用。引力不断改变速度方向，使轨迹弯曲；轨道并不是支撑行星的实体轨道。近似只考虑太阳与一颗行星时，束缚轨道是椭圆，太阳位于一个焦点。开普勒第二定律说明相同时间扫过相同面积，因此同一颗行星接近近日点时通常更快，远离时更慢。

academic.title: 外观、地貌与内部，是不同层次的证据
academic.body: 整球外观有探测影像作为依据，但代表性近景不等于实测着陆地点。地球有岩石与液态水表面，金星有被云遮住的岩石地表；木星、土星、天王星与海王星没有地球式的固体着陆面。深入巨行星会遇到更高的压力和温度。内部剖面综合地震、引力、自转等资料与物理模型；层厚、颜色和候选边界是讲解方式，不能当作透视照片。太阳的光球也不是岩石地面，深处的核聚变为它提供能量。

academic.title: 同一幅图中的动态，不一定共用物理时钟
academic.body: 太阳系公转模式保留行星周期关系；卫星模式也在一个共同的模拟时钟下按周期绕行，但两者的显示时间不相同。大气流动和太阳活动是连续的现象示意，不是天气预测或磁流体计算。下降进度控制观察相机，与现象动态分开暂停；其百分比不是高度、时间或压力测量。卫星大小与轨道间距分别调整，环是颗粒群，卫星则是一个个绕行天体。月相属于观察方向与照明几何的另一个问题，保留专门的后续入口。

zh.misconception: 蓝色不一定是水，亮云不一定是地面；太阳不是燃烧的岩石球，卫星也不是另一类行星。
zh.boundary: 代表性地形、气象与太阳活动经过简化；下降不是可生存飞行、自由落体计算或实时观测。大小比较单独保持直径比例，剖面厚度和卫星系统显示尺度均为示意。

narration.label: 认识一大家子
narration.text: 让我们从太阳旁边出发。太阳会自己发光，八颗行星围着它走。离太阳近的有水星、金星、地球和火星；再往外，还有木星、土星、天王星和海王星。先别急着记名字，挑一个你喜欢的世界，看看它在哪一圈。
narration.cue: 显示轨道全景，停在初始位置。

narration.label: 向下看，会遇见什么
narration.text: 选中地球，从太空慢慢往下看。先看到一整颗蓝色星球，再靠近白云，最后靠近选定区域的沙丘或冰面。随时停下来看看：云会走，下面的陆地没有跟着云一起走。现在换成木星，你还会找到一块能站住的地面吗？它的条纹和旋涡是大气，越往下，周围越浓。
narration.cue: 地球下降依次停在全景、云层和近景；再选择木星，比较终点。

narration.label: 太阳也在变化
narration.text: 回到太阳身边。它自己发光，深处的核聚变不断释放能量。看，表面似乎有许多小小的明暗颗粒，还有较暗的黑子。黑子只是比周围冷，仍然热得惊人。边缘的弧线代表日珥，太阳物质受到磁场约束。我们可以暂停画面寻找这些结构，但那里没有能站立的地面。
narration.cue: 选择太阳，播放后暂停，指出颗粒、黑子与日珥；切换内部到核心。

narration.label: 星球身边的小伙伴
narration.text: 地球有月球，土星身边也有许多卫星。它们绕着行星走，又和行星一起绕太阳。选择土卫六，跟着它从土星旁边来到浓雾下的世界。这里的湖主要装着甲烷和乙烷，不是水。看完再退回土星，你会发现：近处的世界和远处的太阳系，原来是连在一起的。
narration.cue: 地月与土星系统之间比较；进入土卫六，再通过父级按钮返回土星。

en.question: If we descend from space, will every world eventually reveal ground to stand on?
en.observe: Compare orbits and sizes, then select Earth, play cloud activity and choose a desert or ice-sheet site and scrub the descent. Try Jupiter’s storms and deeper atmosphere, find solar spots and prominences, then enter Titan from Saturn and return to its parent system.

academic.title: An orbit is a continuously turning path
academic.body: A planet moves while the Sun’s gravity changes its velocity, bending its path. There is no physical rail underneath it. In the two-body approximation a bound orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at a focus. Equal areas are swept out in equal times, so a planet usually moves faster near perihelion and slower near aphelion.

academic.title: Appearance, terrain and interiors use different evidence
academic.body: Whole-globe appearance is informed by spacecraft images, but a representative close view is not a surveyed landing site. Earth has rocky and liquid-water surfaces; Venus has rock hidden beneath clouds. The four giant planets have no Earth-like solid landing surface. Going deeper raises pressure and temperature. Cutaways combine seismic, gravity, rotation and physical-model constraints; thicknesses, colors and candidate boundaries are teaching devices, not photographs. The solar photosphere is not rocky ground either; fusion deep inside powers the Sun.

academic.title: Different animated views need different clocks
academic.body: The orbit view preserves relative planetary periods. Moon views also use a shared clock and relative periods, but on a separate display timescale. Atmospheric flows and solar activity are continuous illustrations, not forecasts or magnetohydrodynamic calculations. Descent controls the observation camera and pauses independently of activity; its percentage is not a height, time or pressure measurement. Moon sizes and orbital spacing are scaled separately. Rings are particle populations; moons are individual orbiting bodies. Phases are a separate question about viewing and illumination geometry, with their own follow-up topic.

en.misconception: Blue does not necessarily mean water, and bright clouds are not ground. The Sun is not burning rock, and moons are not another class of planet.
en.boundary: Terrain, weather and solar activity are simplified illustrations. Descent is not a survivable flight, free-fall calculation or live observation. The size comparison alone preserves diameter ratios; cutaway thicknesses and moon-system display scales are schematic.

narration.label: Meet the family
narration.text: Let’s begin beside the Sun. The Sun makes its own light, and eight planets travel around it. Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are closer in. Farther out are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. You do not have to remember every name yet. Choose a world you like and find its path.

narration.label: What will we meet below?
narration.text: Choose Earth and descend slowly from space. First comes the whole blue globe, then white clouds, and finally dunes or ice at the selected site. Pause and look: clouds move while land stays beneath them. Now try Jupiter. Will you find ground to stand on? Its bands and swirls are atmosphere, which becomes denser farther down.
narration.cue: Pause Earth’s descent at the globe, clouds and close view. Compare the endpoint on Jupiter.

narration.label: The Sun changes too
narration.text: Return to the Sun. It shines with energy released by fusion deep inside. Look for small bright and dark granules and darker sunspots. Sunspots are cooler than their surroundings, but still extremely hot. Arches at the edge represent prominences, where magnetic fields support solar material. Pause to inspect them. There is no solid ground here.
narration.cue: Play and pause solar activity. Identify granules, spots and prominences, then inspect the fusion core.

narration.label: Companions around planets
narration.text: Earth has the Moon, and Saturn has many moons too. They orbit their planets and travel with them around the Sun. Choose Titan and approach its hazy world. Its lakes contain mainly methane and ethane, not water. Return to Saturn afterward. The close world and the distant solar system belong to the same connected place.
narration.cue: Compare Earth’s and Saturn’s moon systems, enter Titan, then use the parent button to return.
